subject: Post-demo: model selection & quant tradeoffs for Quartile Health integration
messages:
From: Monica Patel <monica.patel@redwood.ai>

Cc: Neha Kapoor <neha.kapoor@redwood.ai>, Rishi Malhotra <rishi.malhotra@redwood.ai>

Subject: Post-demo: model selection & quant tradeoffs for Quartile Health integration

Hi Eric / Natalie —

Thanks again for the demo today. Quick recap + our recommended next steps while it’s still fresh:

What we heard from Quartile Health:
- Primary workload: clinical note summarization + structured extraction for billing codes (~1.5k tokens typical context).
- SLA targets: 95th perc latency under 350ms for single-request generation; offline batch ok for heavy reports.
- Quality sensitivity: hallucination tolerance is low for extraction; summaries can be permissive if highlighted.

Preliminary model recommendations (subject to evaluation):
- Candidate A: Mistral-instruct-7B (FP16) — best accuracy/latency balance in our internal checks for short-context extraction.
- Candidate B: Llama-2-13B-AWQ — attractive cost/throughput with AWQ quant; we saw small regression on numerics in some prompt templates.
- Candidate C: Redwood-3B-optimized (FP8-profile) — very low latency, good for high-throughput routing as a first-pass.

Quantization and throughput notes (high level):
- AWQ: excellent memory reduction, usually minimal semantic drop for instruction tasks but can be model-dependent.
- GPTQ: more conservative; sometimes preserves numeric fidelity better than AWQ in our tests.
- FP8: great latency but requires careful calibration; expect occasional tokenization artifacts on long tails.

Attachments I’m including: promptset_v2.jsonl (the prompts we used in today’s demo), quartile_requirements_matrix.xlsx (your SLOs + data sensitivity), and a bench summary we’ll expand on.

Proposed next steps:
1) Agreement on two test prompts and three extraction templates from your side (can use the attached promptset_v2 as a starting point).
2) Redwood runs a controlled bench across the three candidate variants (AWQ/GPTQ/FP8) using your prompts — target turnaround 48 hours.
3) Post-bench call to review regressions, latency profiles, and pick a canary config.

If that sounds good I’ll loop in Vivek to schedule the bench and get an initial HubSpot playbook set up.

Best,
Monica Patel
Enterprise Sales
Redwood Inference

Thanks Monica — this is helpful. A couple clarifying Qs from our end:

1) On latency: 350ms 95th is a hard bar for interactive triage workflows. What hardware baseline are you assuming for the AWQ/GPTQ/FP8 runs?
2) On quality: when you say "small regression on numerics" for the Llama-2-13B-AWQ, can you quantify (e.g., % failure on code extraction tests)? We can tolerate slight drops on freeform summaries but not on billing code extraction.
3) Compliance: does the bench run live on our VPC (preferred) or on Redwood hosted infra? We need bench artifacts for our security review.

Also looping in our procurement alias (procure@quartilehealth.com) to flag potential timelines for PO if we move forward.

Subject: Bench plan + initial numbers (attached)

Hi Eric / Natalie —

Thanks — answered inline:
1) Hardware baseline: For the initial bench we used: NVIDIA A100 80GB (hosted Redwood infra) and a mirror run on a dedicated T4 cluster for throughput estimates. If you prefer VPC, we can run the same rig in your VPC (requires short setup).

2) Numeric/extraction regressions: For Llama-2-13B-AWQ on our clinical extraction promptset we saw ~3.8% drop in exact-match code extraction relative to FP16 baseline (n=1,200 prompts). GPTQ variants tended to show ~1.2% drop; FP8-profile (Redwood-3B-optimized) had <1% on structured fields but lower recall on edge-case long spans. Detailed CSV attached.

3) Compliance/artifacts: We can run the bench in your VPC and deposit the raw logs + bench CSV to a shared Drive link (we’ll also provide checksums).

Quick behavioral notes from the run:
- AWQ: faster token throughput (up to 2.6x vs FP16 under continuous batching) but occasional tokenization misalignments for certain de-identified IDs.
- GPTQ: slightly slower but more stable numerics in extraction fields.
- FP8-profile (Redwood-3B): excellent latency, best cost, recommended as a first-line filter in a routing pipeline (low-risk extractions still require FP16/GPTQ verification for high-sensitivity fields).

I’ve attached: redwood_bench_20260317.csv and bench_notes_awq_vs_gptq.pdf — see the CSV for per-template EM scores and latency percentiles.

If you’d like, we can also include a small AB test plan to surface regressions on your live data while keeping a manual fallback gating step.

Regards,
Neha Kapoor
Solutions Architect, Redwood Inference

Subject: Re: Bench plan + initial numbers (attached)

Eric — quick technical addendum to help you weigh AWQ vs GPTQ vs FP8 for the extraction workload:

- Evaluation metrics to prioritize: exact-match (EM) for code extraction, false-positive rate (FPR) for hallucinated codes, and 95th perc latency. For Quartile we recommend EM > 98% for critical fields.
- Canary strategy: start with Redwood-3B FP8 as a high-throughput filter; route uncertain/confidence<0.85 cases to Llama-2-13B-GPTQ; reserve FP16 Mistral-instruct for final authoritative calls where the token window or stakes are high.
- Calibration: AWQ weights often require per-prompt calibration — we build a tiny per-template bias table which improved EM by ~0.9% in our runs.
- Monitoring hooks: include per-prompt EM drift alerts and a small human-in-loop queue for the first 2 weeks. If you want, we can push a regression dashboard into your observability stack (we support Splunk/Datadog).

I can produce a short A/B script that runs on 1% of live traffic to measure production drift within your environment — low risk and quick feedback.

-Rishi
Applied ML, Redwood Inference
